intro: The right hand starts with a quick circling figure while the left supplies a longer melodic line. In Rachmaninoff’s own recording, follow how those two kinds of motion exchange prominence and then recede.
question: Can you keep the melody separate from the circling notes?

sections.label: Circling figure and lower melody
sections.mNote: rapid upper notes surround a longer lower line

sections.label: Middle expansion · approximate
sections.mNote: melody and accompaniment change register and weight

sections.label: Opening texture recalled
sections.mNote: quiet upper figuration returns after the central crest

sections.label: Coda · losing momentum
sections.mNote: figures continue while the sound diminishes

cues.title: Two rates of motion
cues.text: The quick right-hand figure is not the main tune. Follow the longer notes beneath it: Rachmaninoff sets a singing line against a more continuous pattern, both held within the score’s compound metre of 12/8.
cues.evidence: Gutheil’s 1911 score, printed p. 48, shows the upper semiquaver figure and lower melodic line in 12/8. The report records substantial onset activity even in the quiet opening; it does not identify individual hands.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A ten-inch Victor side
cues.text: Victor issued this performance on a ten-inch disc, number 64963. The recording register identifies the approved take as the fifth, made in Camden, New Jersey, on 21 January 1921.
cues.evidence: DAHR lists matrix B-24642, take 5, date, place and Victor 64963: https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/refer/700009865. The RCA 1992 booklet gives the same date and matrix for this reissue’s track; the current Archive file is linked by its labelled source chain.

cues.title: Which layer carries the line?
cues.text: Through the middle expansion, listen for the melody changing position relative to the smaller notes. Broken-chord motion can support a more exposed upper line; the accompaniment is no longer confined to its opening role.
cues.evidence: The score’s printed pp. 49–50 transfers continuous figuration into the left hand beneath an upper melodic line before expanding the chords. A boundary at 0:52 and a brief level rise at 0:55 support an approximate middle-region placement.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An older work, a later career
cues.text: The Prelude dates from 1910, but this recording belongs to Rachmaninoff’s career after leaving Russia in 1917. In exile he concentrated increasingly on performing; the recording preserves him revisiting an earlier composition.
cues.evidence: IMSLP dates Op. 32 to 1910. The RCA Complete Recordings booklet, essay “The Composer”, discusses the 1917 departure and subsequent concentration on pianism; its register dates this take to 1921.

cues.title: A quieter return, not an ending
cues.text: After the central crest, the level falls sharply and the opening manner is recalled. Keep following the circling figure: a quieter return still has another rise ahead before the final withdrawal.
cues.evidence: The analysis shows −7 dB at 1:30, then −24.9 at 1:40, with a prominent boundary at 1:36. A second rise reaches −9.8 at 2:00. Score p. 50 supports the recalled upper figuration; its exact first bar is not aligned.

cues.title: Before microphones
cues.text: This is an acoustic recording, made before Victor’s electrical process. The RCA booklet describes separate recording horns for the treble and bass in Rachmaninoff’s acoustic sessions; the piano’s sound was collected mechanically rather than by a microphone.
cues.evidence: The RCA Complete Recordings booklet, essay “The Recordings”, describes the acoustic sessions and separate treble/bass horns. DAHR’s 1921 B-series matrix corroborates the session period; no particular horn arrangement is asserted for this individual take.

cues.title: The figures outlast their force
cues.text: At the close, the little figures continue as the sound weakens. Listen for the difference between moving notes and forward pressure: Rachmaninoff can retain the pattern while allowing the piece to come to rest.
cues.evidence: Score p. 51 marks meno mosso and finally perdendo. The strongest analysis boundary is 2:20; level falls from −21.4 dB at 2:15 to −39 at 2:25, with onset activity down to 0.2 per second at 2:30.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The moving figure changes its job
transitions.how: The opening’s upper figure is loosened and redistributed. In the contrasting passage, the left hand supplies a more continuous broken-chord accompaniment while the right hand projects longer melodic notes. Register and texture, rather than a new instrument or a sudden stop, distinguish the two layers. Subsequent crescendos thicken the line into chords.
transitions.evidence: Gutheil score pp. 49–50: redistribution of figuration and later chordal expansion. The 0:52 boundary and surrounding changes in level provide a provisional time-region anchor; no exact change of hand is claimed at that second.

transitions.title: The crest yields to familiar figuration
transitions.how: The expanded chordal writing subsides and the score restores the small upper figures above a longer lower line. The return recalls the opening’s separation of musical layers, now at a quiet dynamic. It is not yet a coda: Rachmaninoff rebuilds the intensity once more from this recovered texture.
transitions.evidence: The latter part of score p. 50 restores the opening texture quietly and supplies a further crescendo. The prominent 1:36 analysis boundary, level drop across 1:30–1:40 and later 2:00 crest support this broad return region.

transitions.title: The pattern diminishes without disappearing
transitions.how: A final expansion gives way to meno mosso and a longer-held bass. The upper figures continue over that steadier foundation, but the direction is now towards reduced volume and fewer emphatic arrivals. The last perdendo marking extends the withdrawal: Rachmaninoff retains the figuration while draining its momentum.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 51 contains meno mosso, extended bass notes and perdendo. The analysis declines from −9.8 dB at 2:00 to −20.4 at 2:10, with a boundary at 2:08 and a stronger closing boundary at 2:20.

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Interview with Leonard Liebling, The Musical Courier, 1939

composer.background:
Rachmaninoff learnt the sound of Russian worship before he learnt orchestration. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where unaccompanied voices and bells occupied different parts of the ceremony: chant inside the church, metal sounding above and outside it. His music repeatedly brings the two together. A melody moves in narrow steps while bass notes toll beneath it; a chord is struck again before its previous resonance has died. The C♯ minor Prelude, the Second Piano Concerto and The Bells make this audible without requiring an actual church bell. The All-Night Vigil removes the instruments altogether, leaving a choir to produce both the sustained line and the accumulating weight of the harmony.

Born into a landowning family in 1873, he spent his early childhood at Oneg, near Novgorod. His father’s financial failures brought the sale of the estates and a move to St Petersburg. Rachmaninoff entered its Conservatory in 1883, but his general schoolwork deteriorated; his parents separated, and his sister Sofia died of diphtheria. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended a transfer to Moscow and the supervision of Nikolai Zverev. The move exchanged a disorganised household for one in which practice, meals and attendance at concerts were regulated by a piano teacher.
composer.epithet: A composer-pianist who built long melodies over tolling basses, and carried Russian chant into the concertos and dances of his American exile.
